title: Microsoft disrupts AI-assisted platform that compromised 12,000 accounts
gist: Microsoft led an industry disruption of EvilTokens, a Telegram-distributed subscription cybercrime platform ($1,500 setup plus $500/month) that used an AI chatbot to analyze compromised inboxes and automate business email compromise fraud, seizing 200 domains/websites and compromising 12,000 Microsoft accounts across 10,000 organizations before UK police made two arrests; Microsoft says the AI-driven approach compressed the time to exploit a compromised inbox from days to minutes.

insights.claim: EvilTokens was introduced over a Telegram channel in February 2026, charging an initial $1,500 fee plus a recurring $500 monthly charge, and provided a single integrated service for compromising email accounts, analyzing inboxes for high-value targets, and drafting realistic fraud follow-up emails.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Quantifies the commercial 'cybercrime-as-a-service' pricing model ($1,500 upfront + $500/month), useful for benchmarking the economics of AI-enabled fraud platforms against the scale of damage they can cause.
insights.locator: Named EvilTokens, the platform was introduced over a Telegram channel

insights.claim: At the center of EvilTokens was an AI-style chatbot that could analyze a victim's inbox to identify trusted relationships, payment authorizations, and sensitive responsibilities, and could recommend fraud strategies including drafting messages impersonating trusted contacts.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Demonstrates a concrete, operational example of generative AI being weaponized to automate business email compromise (BEC) fraud at scale, a direct case study for the dual-use risk of AI language models in cybercrime.
insights.quote: at the center of the service was an AI-style chatbot that could analyze a victim’s inbox and help criminals identify trusted relationships, payment authorizations, and sensitive responsibilities
insights.locator: “While EvilTokens helped cybercriminals access email accounts

insights.claim: EvilTokens analyzed 5,000 compromised emails at a time, using AI to identify employees authorized to disburse large sums, the managers they reported to, and convincing scenarios under which those employees could be persuaded to transfer money into attacker-controlled accounts.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Quantifies the batch-processing scale (5,000 emails at once) of the AI analysis pipeline, illustrating the throughput advantage AI gives attackers over manual inbox review.
insights.locator: A dashboard allowed users to tailor lures

insights.claim: Account compromises were achieved through abuse of a legitimate OAuth device code authentication flow (designed for TVs and input-constrained devices) against Microsoft Entra; victims who clicked malicious email links were directed to a webpage running a hidden automation script that generated a device code in real time, which victims were then tricked into entering on the official Microsoft device login portal, with complex Node.js backend logic helping the platform evade signature- or pattern-based detection.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Details a specific, technical attack-chain exploit (device code phishing against OAuth flows) that security teams and Microsoft Entra administrators should specifically monitor and harden against, since it bypasses conventional detection methods.
insights.locator: Account compromises were achieved through a legitimate OAuth process

themes.theme: Scale of the disruption and impact

insights.claim: EvilTokens users compromised 12,000 customer accounts belonging to 10,000 organizations worldwide, with the highest concentration in the US, followed by Canada, the UK, Australia, India, and France; victim organizations spanned wholesale distribution, construction, financial services, real estate, higher education, and healthcare.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete victim count (12,000 accounts, 10,000 organizations) and sector/geographic spread, useful for assessing the real-world scale of AI-assisted BEC fraud and which sectors face elevated exposure.
insights.locator: Microsoft said users of EvilToken compromised 12,000 customer accounts

insights.claim: Using legal process and a network of partners, Microsoft seized 50 websites and 150 additional domains used to operate EvilTokens, and the UK's Metropolitan Police Service arrested two men on suspicion of offenses connected to the platform.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Confirms the takedown achieved concrete enforcement outcomes (200 domains/sites seized, two arrests), a positive data point on industry-law enforcement collaboration effectiveness against AI-enabled cybercrime platforms.
insights.locator: Using a legal process and a network of partners

themes.theme: Strategic implications of AI in cybercrime

insights.claim: Microsoft says EvilTokens represents a major shift in mass account compromise because it previously took attackers significant time to manually sift through thousands of emails to map an organization's management chart, suppliers, customers, and relationships — a burden AI-assisted tools greatly reduce.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Articulates the core structural threat AI poses in cybercrime: automating what was previously the most labor-intensive and time-consuming part of targeted fraud (organizational reconnaissance), compressing attacker cost and time-to-exploit.
insights.locator: Microsoft said that EvilTokens represents a major shift

insights.claim: Microsoft warns organizations that once an inbox is compromised, criminals may now understand its contents in minutes rather than days, and recommends independently verifying requests to change payment information, redirect funds, or approve unusual transactions through a trusted second channel, in addition to strong identity protections and monitoring.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A direct, actionable security recommendation (second-channel verification for payment changes) that organizations should adopt given AI-compressed attacker response times, relevant guidance for enterprise security policy and vendor risk management.
insights.quote: assume that once an inbox is compromised, criminals may understand its contents in minutes, not days
